market_scan.market_size_text: The global industrial drying equipment market is ~$5-10B/yr depending on scope (FactMR ~$4.8B 2025; GrandView ~$8.2B 2025; SNS ~$14B 2023), with rotary dryers ~$1.3-4B of that and minerals/ores ~24% of rotary dryer demand. So the mineral drying equipment+services pool relevant here is order-of-magnitude ~$1-3B/yr globally. The underlying product markets are much larger (kaolin ~46 Mt/yr, ~$5-8B; GCC ~$12-21B; ore concentrates far bigger), and drying consumes 10-25% of industrial energy — mostly fossil-fired today. Electrification is at pilot/early-reference stage (Mondo Minerals talc 5 MW electric heater, Nordic Mining electric dryers, Fraunhofer SHS+MVR), so the 'electrified mineral drying' market itself is emerging, worth low $ hundreds of millions and policy-driven.

regions.Europe: ~$0.3-0.8B (~20% of mineral dryer spend; strongest electrification pull from ETS/gas prices)
regions.Asia: ~$1-2B (~40-48% share, China/India; mostly new-build, weaker electrification economics)
regions.America: ~$0.5-1.2B (~25-30%; US IRA/DOE funding supports electrification pilots)

market_scan.target_customers_text: A few thousand thermal-drying plants worldwide: Europe alone has ~750 processing plants and 685 mines/quarries among IMA-Europe's 250 member companies (180 Mt/yr minerals). Decision-making is concentrated in majors — Omya runs ~160 plants, Imerys ~100+ sites (48 for CaCO3 alone) — so a handful of corporate engineering/sustainability teams controls a large share of the reachable base; below that sits a long tail of regional and single-quarry operators that are cheap to ignore and hard to sell to. Ore concentrators (copper, iron, nickel laterite, rutile/garnet) add several hundred single-line drying assets with high per-site value. Buyers respond to carbon cost (EU ETS), gas-price volatility, and net-zero commitments; procurement cycles are slow (12-24 months) and references matter.
market_scan.players_text: Incumbent thermal dryer supply is moderately concentrated at the top (top-5 rotary-dryer OEMs ~35-52% of revenue depending on report) but fragmented below, with strong regional and niche OEMs plus aggressive Chinese suppliers. None of the large OEMs leads in electric/microwave drying — the dielectric niche is a field of SMEs (SAIREM, Pueschner, Cellencor, Ferrite/IMS, Muegge, Fricke & Mallah) offering 6-300 kW modules, and utilities/ESCOs (e.g. Nevel) are entering electrification-as-a-service. Whitespace: no dominant MW-scale electric dryer vendor for bulk minerals yet.
players: turnkey rotary/fluid-bed/flash dryer lines integrated with grinding, mostly gas/oil-fired; growing service/efficiency-retrofit offers
Medium (Allgaier, Comessa, Schenck, Carrier Vibrating, FEECO, Hazemag, Mitchell, Louisville, Buehler, Chinese OEMs)
standard and custom rotary/FBD dryers, regional service, price-competitive
Small electric/dielectric niche (SAIREM, Pueschner, Cellencor, Ferrite/IMS, Muegge; ESCOs like Nevel)
kW-to-300 kW microwave/RF dryers, electric air/SHS heating, electrification projects
regulation: Dryers are explicitly listed combustion units in Annex I; installations >20 MWth pay per tCO2 (~EUR60-90/t recently). Electrifying drying removes the exposure directly.
Free allowances shrink for CBAM sectors and benchmarks tighten elsewhere, raising the effective carbon cost of gas-fired drying for EU mineral producers.
Gas burners of 1-50 MW need permits and NOx/SOx/dust limits; electric heating exits combustion permitting entirely, simplifying new lines.
EU 2040 climate target / Net-Zero Industry Act
Communication targets ~80% fossil-fuel cut by 2040; process-heat electrification is a named lever and benefits from NZIA/Innovation Fund support.
Mandatory audits/energy-management systems flag drying (10-25% of industrial energy) as a priority action at every large mineral site.
National & US incentives (Germany EEW/carbon contracts, EU Innovation Fund; US IRA 48C, DOE industrial demos)
Subsidies and contracts-for-difference specifically fund switching fossil process heat to electric — de-risks customer capex for an electric dryer.

technologies.name: Direct-fired rotary dryer (incumbent)
technologies.how: Gas/oil burner heats air blown through a rotating drum; co- or counter-current contact evaporates moisture from bulk solids.
technologies.performance: ~3,500-9,000 kJ/kg water (~1.0-2.5 kWh/kg); BEE field data 788-1,416 kcal/kg; units 20-100+ t/h; ~30-60% thermal efficiency vs 0.63 kWh/kg latent floor.
technologies.limits: Fossil heat source with exhaust losses; EU ETS/MCPD burden; 'electrifying' it means bolting on resistive/H2 burners with unchanged air losses.

technologies.name: Fluid-bed dryer (incumbent)
technologies.how: Hot gas fluidizes fine particles through a perforated plate/distributor for high heat/mass transfer.
technologies.performance: ~4,000-6,000 kJ/kg water (~1.1-1.7 kWh/kg); single units to ~64-128 t/h on ore concentrates (e.g. Asarco copper).
technologies.limits: Needs fluidizable particle size; high fan power; still gas-fired air heaters; fines entrainment/dust load.

technologies.name: Flash/pneumatic dryer (incumbent)
technologies.how: Wet fines dispersed in a hot gas stream, drying in seconds; often integrated in the grinding mill circuit.
technologies.performance: Very high evaporation flux (~750 kg/m2h); e.g. Mondo Minerals talc flash drying at ~450C air, ~20 GWh/yr site demand.
technologies.limits: Surface moisture on fine powders only; high exhaust-volume losses; fossil-fired today.

technologies.name: Spray dryer (incumbent, slurries)
technologies.how: Kaolin/mineral slurry atomized into hot air to make dry powder directly.
technologies.performance: 4,500-11,500 kJ/kg water (~1.3-3.2 kWh/kg) — the most energy-hungry dryer type; standard for slurry feeds.
technologies.limits: Only viable for pumpable slurries; huge air heating duty makes electrification hard except via SHS/heat-pump routes.

technologies.name: Superheated-steam drying + MVR/heat pump (emerging electric rival)
technologies.how: Closed steam loop dries material; mechanical vapor recompression recovers latent heat electrically (Fraunhofer LowCarbDry).
technologies.performance: Targets 2-4x lower energy than hot-air drying; heat-pump drying ~0.14-0.31 kWh/kg water; ~4000 h demo operation reported in H2020 DryFiciency.
technologies.limits: TRL ~5-6, pilot scale; compressor capex; steam chemistry/corrosion; unproven on abrasive bulk minerals.

technologies.name: Microwave/RF dielectric drying (ProSeed)
technologies.how: 915/2450 MHz fields volumetrically and selectively heat water inside the solid; energy deposited in the product, not in air.
technologies.performance: Measured on iron pellets: ~120 vs ~170 kWh/t product (-30%) and 6-13x faster than convective; drying efficiency up to 56-78% vs ~30% convective; tailings >50% energy cut. Modules 6-300 kW (SAIREM, Pueschner, Ferrite/IMS).
technologies.limits: Low-dielectric-loss matrices dry poorly (silica sand DE ~40%); multi-MW scale-up unproven commercially; electricity costs ~3-5x gas per kWh — economics hinge on efficiency gain + carbon price.

tech_baseline.why_better_text: Microwave drying deposits energy directly in the water inside the solid instead of heating tonnes of air and losing it in the exhaust — measured 30-50% lower specific energy on iron pellets and tailings at pilot scale. Being fully electric, it exits EU ETS and combustion-permitting scope, can run on renewable PPAs for scope-1-zero product claims (Mondo Minerals and Nordic Mining already proved this buyer logic with conventional electric heating), and offers instant controllability for demand response. Incumbents are ~30-60% thermally efficient against a 0.63 kWh/kg latent floor, leaving real headroom; the open question is scale-up economics versus cheap gas.
key_assumptions: Drying = ~10-25% of industrial energy consumption, and mineral dryers today are overwhelmingly gas/oil-fired (measured, literature/industry).
Incumbent rotary/fluid-bed dryers use ~1.0-2.5 kWh_th per kg water vs 0.63 kWh/kg latent minimum, i.e. >=30% efficiency headroom for any better technology (measured).

Microwave drying saves ~30-50% energy vs convective on iron pellets/tailings (measured, pilot); kaolin/CaCO3 dielectric response likely between silica sand (DE ~40%, poor) and iron ore/basalt (DE ~65-78%, good) — must be measured per product (assumed).

A 50 t/h line drying 10%->0.5% moisture evaporates ~5 t/h water ~3-4 MW_th; commercial MW modules today top out ~300 kW, so ~10x array scale-up is needed — an engineering, not physics, gap (measured + assumed).
Economics work where carbon-priced gas plus ETS (~EUR60-90/tCO2) meets renewable electricity <~EUR80-100/MWh; strongest in EU/Nordics, weakest on cheap coal gas in Asia (assumed).
